advances:
This gives the sharp symbolic chord-concavity inequality, including the
regimes \(b\le\lambda\delta\), zero traces, and support-boundary traces.  In
the canonical common-order support it yields three explicit lower bounds on
the \(A_0\) traces.  Those three bounds, the crossing equalities, the
canonical tails, and \(W=0\) are jointly consistent: an exact rational
\(A_0\) from accepted fact `331355cde8383f52` realizes all three cyclic
inequalities strictly, and its cell areas admit the exact positive scalar
completion given below.  Thus these three inequalities and the scalar
identities do not force a row exclusion.
The next missing coupling is geometric: one common \(A_2\) must realize the
completion areas and global lower crossings while retaining the three traces
and the support-gap direction, and one common \(K\) must then contain the
midpoint body with the completed middle-cell areas.

proof:
Let
\[
w(y)=\mathcal H^1\{X:(X,y)\in A\}
\]
be the horizontal chord length.  It is concave on the vertical support
interval of \(A\).  First suppose \(a_->0\) and \(b>0\).  Then \(Y=0\)
lies in the interior of that interval, the actual chord length equals
\(\lambda\), and the finite right derivative
\[
g=w'_+(0)
\]
is a supergradient.  Hence
\[
w(y)\le\lambda+gy
\tag{6}
\]
throughout the support interval.

Because \(B\subset\{0<Y<\delta\}\),
\[
b\le\int_0^\delta w(y)\,dy.
\tag{7}
\]
If \(b>\lambda\delta\), (6)-(7) force \(g>0\) and give
\[
g\ge\frac{2(b-\lambda\delta)}{\delta^2}.
\tag{8}
\]
For \(y<0\), nonnegativity and (6) show that the support cannot extend
below \(-\lambda/g\).  Therefore
\[
a_-
\le\int_{-\lambda/g}^0(\lambda+gy)\,dy
=\frac{\lambda^2}{2g}
\le
\frac{\lambda^2\delta^2}
{4(b-\lambda\delta)}.
\]
This proves (1) when its left side is nonzero.  If
\(b\le\lambda\delta\), its left side vanishes.  If \(a_-=0\), the
inequality is also immediate and \(\lambda\) is interpreted from the
interior side of the support line.  If \(\lambda=0\) and \(a_->0\),
concavity and nonnegativity prevent positive width on both sides of
zero, so \(b=0\); this is exactly (3).  These observations cover all
boundary cases.

The estimate is sharp as a statement forced only by chord concavity.
Suppose first that \(\lambda>0\) and \(b>\lambda\delta\).  Put
\[
\gamma=\frac{2(b-\lambda\delta)}{\delta^2}.
\]
For any
\[
0<a_-\le\frac{\lambda^2}{2\gamma},
\]
put
\[
\eta=\frac{\lambda^2}{2a_-}\ge\gamma
\]
and take a chord profile whose consecutive affine pieces are
\[
w(y)=\lambda+\eta y
\quad\left(-\frac{\lambda}{\eta}\le y\le0\right),
\qquad
w(y)=\lambda+\gamma y
\quad(0\le y\le\delta),
\]
followed by any affine descent to zero with slope at most \(\gamma\).
The slopes are nonincreasing, so \(w\) is concave.  The region
\[
\{(X,Y):0\le X\le w(Y)\}
\]
is a convex polygon, its area below zero is \(a_-\), and its strip area
on \(0<Y<\delta\) is exactly \(b\).  Equality in (2) occurs when
\(\eta=\gamma\).  The case \(a_-=0\) starts the support at zero.

If \(\lambda>0\) and \(b\le\lambda\delta\), use an arbitrary
\(\eta>0\) below zero and the constant profile \(w=\lambda\) on
\([0,\delta]\).  Then \(a_-=\lambda^2/(2\eta)\) can be any positive
number, while a central subcell of any area
\(0\le b\le\lambda\delta\) fits in the strip.  When \(\lambda=0\),
a triangle opening above zero realizes \(a_-=0,b>0\), and its reflection
realizes \(a_->0,b=0\).  Thus (1) is the strongest relation among
\(a_-,b,\lambda,\delta\) obtainable from chord concavity alone.

For the canonical specialization, use \(Y=p_i\).  On \(P_0\), all
three \(p\)-coordinates are positive and sum to \(\delta\), so
\[
P_0\subset\{0<p_i<\delta\}.
\]
Coordinate area is \(\Delta\) times physical area.  The areas below
\(p_i=0\) are respectively
\[
\Delta a,\qquad \Delta d,\qquad \Delta(c+d).
\]
Substitution in (1) gives (4j)-(4l).  Writing
\[
r=\lambda_{0i}\delta
\]
and \(u=u_i\), the nonvacuous part becomes
\[
r^2+4\Delta u\,r-4\Delta^2ub\ge0.
\]
Its nonnegative root is
\[
2\Delta\left(\sqrt{u(u+b)}-u\right),
\]
which proves (5); the root is strictly below \(\Delta b\), so the same
bound also includes the vacuous regime \(r\ge\Delta b\).

We now give the exact surviving regime.  Use the rational polygon
\[
A_0=\operatorname{conv}\left\{
\left(-\frac{21}{71},\frac{43}{142}\right),
\left(\frac3{10},\frac7{10}\right),
\left(\frac45,\frac35\right),
\left(\frac{29}{19},-\frac3{133}\right)
\right\}
\tag{9}
\]
from accepted fact `331355cde8383f52`.  Here
\[
\delta=\frac32,\qquad \Delta=1,
\]
\[
a=\frac{21}{568},\qquad
b=\frac{27}{50},\qquad
c=\frac1{920},\qquad
d=\frac1{24472},
\tag{10}
\]
and
\[
\lambda_{0j}=\frac14,\qquad
\lambda_{0k}=\frac1{46},\qquad
\lambda_{0\ell}=\frac1{10}.
\tag{11}
\]
It has exactly the required common-order \(P\)-support.  The three
cyclic inequalities are strict:
\[
\frac{693}{113600}<\frac9{256},
\qquad
\frac{1167}{56285600}<\frac9{33856},
\qquad
\frac{117}{266000}<\frac9{1600},
\tag{12}
\]
where the left and right sides are respectively the two sides of
(4j), (4k), and (4l).

The same \(A_0\) cell areas admit the following exact positive scalar
completion.  Put
\[
H=\frac{2b-5c-14d}{5}
=\frac{93867}{437000}
\]
and assign
\[
e=\frac c2+2d=\frac{153}{244720},\qquad
g_0=y=\frac c2=\frac1{1840},\qquad
g=z=d=\frac1{24472},\qquad
s=a=\frac{21}{568},
\tag{13}
\]
\[
x=H-a-e=\frac{76972473}{434378000},
\qquad
w=H-a-d=\frac{2032271}{11431000}.
\tag{14}
\]
All eight quantities in (13)-(14) are positive.  They satisfy
\[
c=g_0+y,\qquad
a+e+x=H=d+s+w.
\tag{15}
\]
Consequently the three canonical crossing sums are all
\[
t=H+c+g+z
=\frac{165161}{764750}.
\tag{16}
\]
For the common-order support, (15) also reduces the \(W\)-identity to
\[
W=5(H+c)+7(g+z)-2b=0
\tag{17}
\]
by the definition of \(H\).  Hence (16) equals
\[
\frac{2(M+m+\kappa)}9.
\]
The canonical tails hold because
\[
s=a,\qquad e=d+y+d>d+y,
\]
and the three strict second-tail margins are
\[
b-2d,\qquad b+\frac c2-d,\qquad b-d,
\]
all positive.  Moreover
\[
M=\frac{1091799}{1888600}
>
m=\frac{331703}{8687560},
\qquad
0<t<M,
\]
and all finite-interior inequalities follow from positivity of every
listed cell.

Thus the three sharp chord inequalities and all canonical scalar
equalities leave an exact nonempty regime anchored by the actual polygon
(9).  Accepted fact `331355cde8383f52` further supplies, for this same
\(A_0\), an actual \(A_2\) with strict trace domination in all three
directions and support gap
\[
\frac{3429}{1775}<2
\]
in the positive direction \((1,7/5)\).  That certified \(A_2\) does not
have the completion areas (13), so these two pieces must not be conflated
into a full realization.

The unresolved coupling is now exact.  One must construct or exclude a
single convex \(A_2\) that simultaneously has the four areas in (13),
globally realizes all three lower crossings against (9), retains the
paired traces relative to the three \(A_0\) traces in (11), and satisfies
one positive support-gap inequality
from accepted fact `331355cde8383f52`.  Only after that can one ask for a
single convex \(K\) containing \((A_0+A_2)/2\) with the middle areas
(14).  Neither the three inequalities (4j)-(4l) nor the crossing and
\(W\) identities couple these requirements.
statement:
Let \(A\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a nonempty compact convex polygon, use
coordinates \((X,Y)\), and let \(\delta>0\).  Let \(B\) be a measurable
central cell contained in
\[
A\cap\{0<Y<\delta\}.
\]
Write
\[
b=|B|,\qquad
a_-=\left|A\cap\{Y<0\}\right|,
\]
and let \(\lambda\ge0\) be the chord trace at \(Y=0\), with the
one-sided interior convention when \(Y=0\) is a support line.  Then
\[
a_-\bigl(b-\lambda\delta\bigr)_+
\le
\frac{\lambda^2\delta^2}{4}.
\tag{1}
\]
Equivalently, if \(b>\lambda\delta\), then
\[
a_-\le
\frac{\lambda^2\delta^2}
{4(b-\lambda\delta)}.
\tag{2}
\]
If \(b\le\lambda\delta\), chord concavity alone gives no finite upper
bound on \(a_-\).  If \(\lambda=0\), (1) reduces to
\[
a_-b=0.
\tag{3}
\]
These cases are sharp using nonnegative concave piecewise-linear chord
profiles, including when \(Y=0\) is a support edge or support vertex.

In the canonical \(A_0\) support, put
\[
\delta=-1-L_j-L_k-L_\ell>0,\qquad
\Delta=|\det(\nabla f_j,\nabla f_k)|,
\]
write \(a,b,c,d\) for the physical areas of
\[
P_j,\quad P_0,\quad P_\ell,\quad P_{k\ell},
\]
and write \(\lambda_{0i}\) for the three coordinate chord traces.
Then the three cyclic instances of (1) are
\[
\Delta a\bigl(\Delta b-\lambda_{0j}\delta\bigr)_+
\le\frac{\lambda_{0j}^2\delta^2}{4},
\tag{4j}
\]
\[
\Delta d\bigl(\Delta b-\lambda_{0k}\delta\bigr)_+
\le\frac{\lambda_{0k}^2\delta^2}{4},
\tag{4k}
\]
\[
\Delta(c+d)\bigl(\Delta b-\lambda_{0\ell}\delta\bigr)_+
\le\frac{\lambda_{0\ell}^2\delta^2}{4}.
\tag{4l}
\]
For \(u_i>0\), where
\[
u_j=a,\qquad u_k=d,\qquad u_\ell=c+d,
\]
each inequality is equivalently the sharp trace lower bound
\[
\lambda_{0i}\delta
\ge
2\Delta\left(\sqrt{u_i(u_i+b)}-u_i\right).
\tag{5}
\]

The inequalities (4j)-(4l), the three canonical crossings, the canonical
tails, and \(W=0\) do not contradict one another.  An exact surviving
scalar/geometric regime is specified in the proof.  It contains an actual
rational common-order polygon \(A_0\), not merely a new scalar area table.
It does not assert a common geometric realization of the completed
\(A_2\) and \(K\) data.
